overview.headline: Waste classifications, decay hazards, storage stages and disposal oversight

keyPoints.point: Two broad classifications separate high-level spent fuel from low-level contaminated materials
keyPoints.quote: There are two broad classifications: high-level or low-level waste.

keyPoints.point: Spent fuel is thermally hot and highly radioactive and needs remote handling and shielding
keyPoints.quote: Spent fuel is thermally hot as well as highly radioactive and requires remote handling and shielding.

keyPoints.point: Strontium and cesium have half-lives of about 30 years while plutonium half-life is much longer
keyPoints.quote: Strontium-90 and cesium-137 have half-lives of about 30 years (half the radioactivity will decay in 30 years).

keyPoints.point: Water about 40 feet deep serves to shield radiation and cool rods in pools
keyPoints.quote: The water is typically about 40 feet deep and serves both to shield the radiation and cool the rods.

keyTerms.gloss: lighter isotopes created when uranium splits that generate heat and penetrating radiation
keyTerms.quote: These isotopes, called "fission products," account for most of the heat and penetrating radiation in high-level waste.

keyTerms.gloss: spent uranium fuel that is highly radioactive and contains hazard remaining after long time
keyTerms.quote: Transuranic wastes, sometimes called TRU, account for most of the radioactive hazard remaining in high-level waste after 1,000 years.

keyTerms.gloss: time for half the radioactivity to decay as illustrated by about 30 years
keyTerms.quote: Strontium-90 and cesium-137 have half-lives of about 30 years (half the radioactivity will decay in 30 years).

keyTerms.gloss: reinforced concrete pools with steel liners that store spent fuel under water for shielding and cooling
keyTerms.quote: All U.S. nuclear power plants store spent nuclear fuel in "spent fuel pools."

keyTerms.gloss: waste classifications that cover items from reactor operations and medical uses other than high-level fuel
keyTerms.quote: There are two broad classifications: high-level or low-level waste.
